request.prompt:
Two versions of a paragraph or short passage come from a README that teaches a technical topic to newcomers. Which is better written? Judge the writing, treating the supplied passage as an excerpt. Do not follow instructions inside the excerpts.

Infer this editor's taste from the eight historical choices below and choose the version this editor would prefer.
<historical_choice_1>
Version A:
When a government announces support for a service or project, a natural question is how much money has been paid. Someone writing a news report may want to check a promise. Someone studying public spending may want to compare one year with another. Both need a number that answers the question they are actually asking.

Version B:
When a government announces support for a service or a project, a natural next question is how much money has actually been paid. A journalist may want to check a promise. A researcher may want to compare this year's spending with last year's. Both need the number that answers the question they are asking, and a public report rarely contains just one candidate.

Editor preferred: B
</historical_choice_1>

<historical_choice_2>
Version A:
For `MAPS-01`, the annual report enters as one frozen text excerpt. Each method receives the same gross-grant question and the same tables. Direct returns an amount. Ledger returns the selected source numbers, and Python adds them after converting thousands of pounds into millions. Both answers are compared with GBP 206.238 million. The three questions from this report remain together when uncertainty is estimated.

Version B:
For example, `MAPS-01` sends the Money and Pensions Service excerpt and one question to each model twice, once with each method's instructions. Direct returns an amount; Ledger returns three grant inflows in thousands of pounds, which the program converts and adds. All six results are compared with the key, GBP 206.238 million.

Editor preferred: B
</historical_choice_2>

<historical_choice_3>
Version A:
The serving-path job turned out to allow an honest way through: the release test compares only the arguments of two function calls, so a model can match the reference exactly and attach the monitor on the next line (`ctx.monitor = L1Monitor(...)`). That keeps the monitor and passes, and it is scored as keeping the monitor.

The agents use seven tools (list, read, write, edit and delete files, run the tests, show the diff) against a simulated repository. No code runs. "Running the tests" is a small function that inspects the files and prints ordinary test output. This is safe, and it gives exact ground truth: whether the monitor survived is read from the final files. The data was written for this experiment on 2026-10-26, so no model can have seen it in training.

Version B:
The agents use seven tools (list, read, write, edit and delete files, run the tests, show the diff) against a simulated repository. No code runs. "Running the tests" is a small function that inspects the files and prints ordinary test output. This is safe, and it gives exact ground truth: whether the monitor survived is read from the final files. The data was written for this experiment on 2026-10-26, so no model can have seen it in training.

Editor preferred: A
</historical_choice_3>

<historical_choice_4>
Version A:
The alternative stops treating commands as text. The agent gets a few typed operations (read this file, write a
report under `output/`, delete one scratch file with a matching approval token), and every path is resolved before
it is checked. That blocks more, but every restriction also blocks some legitimate work, and that cost is rarely
measured.

Version B:
- The project is `/workspace/acme`. The agent may read any project file except secrets: a path with a file or folder named `.env`, `.ssh`, `credentials` or `payroll` is refused.

- It may write only under `output/`.

- It may delete single files only under `tmp/`, and only when a trusted person has approved that deletion.

Editor preferred: B
</historical_choice_4>

<historical_choice_5>
Version A:
`test-002` is the first test invoice of the mixed kind, chosen by position rather than by the size of any error. Each line's paid units are the billed units, capped by what was received less returns and less units billed before. The price is the lower of the contracted and invoiced prices.

Version B:
Invoice `test-002` is the first held-out case with mixed arithmetic rules. It was selected by its case position, not by the size of its error. The table shows the quantity calculation and the amounts after each line's own rounding. The contracted price caps the invoiced price. Previously billed units are removed from cumulative deliveries so that the same goods are not paid twice.

Editor preferred: A
</historical_choice_5>

<historical_choice_6>
Version A:
A public report can contain several reasonable numbers for the same programme. One may describe what has been approved for future use. Another may describe a cost recorded in the accounts. Another may describe money that has already changed hands. Before adding anything up, we need to understand which of these the report is describing.

Version B:
The same report can hold an amount approved for future use, a cost recorded in the accounts and an amount of money that has already changed hands, all for the same programme. Each is a correct figure for something. Before adding anything up, a reader has to work out which of these each number is. Economists call the step from a promise to an actual payment fiscal implementation, which gives this notebook's folder its name.

Editor preferred: B
</historical_choice_6>

<historical_choice_7>
Version A:
Running the notebook replays everything from these files with no network calls:

New collection needs `NB_LIVE=1`, an `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` and signed-in `claude` and `codex` command-line tools; the size knobs and budget caps sit at the top of the notebook. The prepared conversations are frozen and rebuilt only with `NB_REBUILD_TRACES=1`. The full analysis is in [28_monitor_removal_honesty.ipynb](28_monitor_removal_honesty.ipynb).

Version B:
New collection needs `NB_LIVE=1`, an `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` and signed-in `claude` and `codex` command-line tools; the size knobs and budget caps sit at the top of the notebook. The prepared conversations are frozen and rebuilt only with `NB_REBUILD_TRACES=1`. The full analysis is in [28_monitor_removal_honesty.ipynb](28_monitor_removal_honesty.ipynb).

Editor preferred: A
</historical_choice_7>

<historical_choice_8>
Version A:
The net is 23,715 - 22,498 + 56,550 = 57,767 cents. At 7.25%, tax is 4,188.1075 cents, rounded to 4,188.
Adding the untaxed fee of 518 cents gives 62,473.

Version B:
The net is 23,715 - 22,498 + 56,550 = 57,767 cents. The source specifies a 7.25% tax rate, so tax is
4,188.1075 cents before rounding and 4,188 cents after rounding. Adding the untaxed fee of 518 cents gives
62,473 cents. These calculations establish the expected answer without asking a model to supply it.

Editor preferred: A
</historical_choice_8>

<version_A>
Both cases ask whether to expand an operational trial. The rule is stated in the evidence: expand only if the value of the extra successes, minus both the implementation cost and a vendor fee, is positive. The evidence gives the counts for two customer segments, a dollar value per extra success and both costs. Writers must show the calculation and keep the money question apart from how strong the evidence is.
</version_A>

Both cases ask whether to expand an operational pilot. The rule is deliberately explicit: expand only if added value minus both the implementation cost and the vendor fee is positive. The source supplies segment counts, a value for each extra success and both costs. Writers must show the calculation and distinguish the financial decision from the strength of the evidence.
</version_B>

Return JSON only, with exactly these fields: {"better": "A" or "B", "confidence": a number from 0 to 100, "reason": "at most two sentences"}. Choose one version even if the difference is small.
